instruction: Is writing per-crate onboarding documentation a one-time cleanup task, or something more?
output: It's a standing, permanent responsibility, not a one-time sweep to finish and forget. Whenever a crate's real public API, status, or key gotchas change, its own onboarding doc gets updated in the same session, not deferred. A crate with real, substantial new work and no onboarding doc yet gets one written before moving on. The reason this matters: a session once nearly rebuilt a native training stack from scratch purely because nothing pointed at the fact it already existed, and a separate session spent hours diagnosing real regressions in crates whose stale or missing onboarding docs made the underlying architecture harder to see. Documentation debt is not cosmetic - it directly costs real debugging time later.

instruction: A tiny, few-gram physics body (like an eyeball) seems to be causing large, disproportionate instability in an otherwise-massive (tens of kilograms) simulated body. Real physics, or something else?
output: Investigate for a numerical/architectural cause before assuming real physics. A real, telling test: change the small body's mass toward zero and compare against fully removing that body from the simulation entirely - if both produce nearly identical results, the effect is real (a negligible mass and an absent body are physically equivalent). If the results diverge sharply, or if the relationship between mass and effect is non-monotonic (a middle value performs worse than both a higher and lower value), that is a real tell of numerical/solver conditioning sensitivity to extreme mass ratios between jointed bodies, not genuine physics. Separately, check whether a per-joint calculation (like gravity compensation) is being computed independently at every level of a chain using an overlapping subtree - a small mass at a leaf can get silently recounted at every ancestor's own calculation, compounding a tiny real change into a large apparent one.

instruction: When two active control systems (e.g. two joint motors, or a joint motor and a whole-body stabilizer) each try to independently correct the same shared degree of freedom, what real problem tends to occur, and what is the established fix?
output: They fight each other - a real, measured instability, not just wasted effort. The established fix, seen repeatedly in real, separate subsystems (leg push-off vs. foot-position IK; gaze-driven joint motors vs. a pelvis stabilizer) is to eliminate the competing constraint BY CONSTRUCTION: make the two controllers mutually exclusive rather than simultaneous. Concretely, gate the lower-priority controller to activate only once the higher-priority one has genuinely saturated (reached its own real limit) or released that degree of freedom - never let both apply force to the same DOF in the same tick. This is the real, discrete form of hierarchical task-priority control / null-space projection (Khatib, 1987): a highest-priority task is solved first, and lower-priority tasks are only allowed the 'leftover' capacity.

instruction: In a strict, mutually-exclusive tiered control system (only one tier active at a time, e.g. eyes-then-head-then-body), once a tier saturates and hands off to the next, should its own target keep being recomputed each tick?
output: No - that is a real, easy-to-introduce bug. Once a tier saturates, it must be frozen at its own last real value RELATIVE TO ITS OWN PARENT, and never touched again until a genuinely new episode starts. A tempting but wrong implementation recomputes the saturated tier's 'best effort' target every tick using the live remaining gap - but as an upstream tier (the one now being actively driven) closes that gap, the recomputed value silently drifts back toward center, undoing the freeze. The correct fix uses the tier's own current state as the freeze signal (has it already reached its real limit?) rather than recomputing from the live target-to-current gap, which shrinks for reasons that have nothing to do with that tier's own motion.

instruction: When checking whether a compound structure (e.g. a 'head' made of two separate joints, neck and skull) has used up its full combined range of motion, should the check trigger if ANY ONE sub-joint reaches its own individual limit, or only once ALL of them have?
output: Only once ALL of them have - using OR instead of AND is a real, easy mistake. A root-first (or any single fixed order) allocation algorithm typically maxes out the FIRST joint in its own list before the second joint needs to contribute at all, even when the combined budget genuinely has not been exhausted. Checking 'is the first joint alone at its limit' and treating that as 'the whole compound structure is saturated' triggers a premature escalation - the real remaining capacity in the second joint gets abandoned unused. The correct check requires every real sub-component to independently be at its own limit before treating the whole group as saturated.

instruction: A skeletal animation format stores only bone length and parent, never rotation, for every bone. Is there a valid 'rest pose' - a state where every bone has zero rotation applied?
output: No, and treating zero-rotation as a rest pose is a real mistake, not a simplification. If the format has no independent rest-pose data, every real frame - including a supposed 'standing still' pose - is animation-driven. A renderer showing the mesh with zero rotations applied is displaying an inherently undefined state, not a correctness bug to fix by adjusting the zero pose. The real fix is to pick an actual animation frame as the reference pose - for a character rig, the game's own animation data usually already marks which clip is the canonical idle (sometimes directly, via the animation system's own bytecode/metadata), rather than guessing.

instruction: When retargeting a mesh from one skeleton onto a different, already-animated skeleton (to reuse the second skeleton's real animation clips), what should be preserved and what should be changed?
output: Rescale the target skeleton's bone REST LENGTHS to the source's real proportions, while PRESERVING the target's own existing bone DIRECTIONS. This keeps the target's animation clips valid, since they were authored against those directions, while matching the source's real proportions. Any additional per-piece axis-correction rotation needed to align the source mesh onto the rescaled target must be MEASURED directly - by comparing a real, structurally-meaningful axis (e.g. each rig's own hip-to-spine direction) between the two rigs - never guessed. Guessed axis-fix rotations are a real, recurring, hard-to-diagnose source of visually-wrong-but-technically-valid results.

instruction: A numeric sanity check on an assembled 3D character rig (valid quaternions, plausible bone-length ratios, no NaN) passes cleanly. Is the model visually correct?
output: Not necessarily - a numeric sanity check proves the data isn't a folded-clump-level failure, nothing more. A visible seam between two attached mesh pieces, or a hand rotated 180 degrees at the wrist, passes every quaternion-validity and bone-length-ratio check while still being visibly, obviously wrong. Real visual correctness requires a separate, real image-based check (a fresh render, inspected directly or by an image-capable model) - never claim visual work is finished based on numeric checks alone, and don't trust a written narrative claiming something looks right without re-verifying against a current image.

instruction: Two independently-built projects both hit a 3D character rig that looked correct in isolation but was misaligned once attached to another system, both traced it to a coordinate-axis mismatch, and both converged on the same fix method: compute the real axis directly from the actual mesh/landmark data, verify the predicted error magnitude numerically before trusting the fix, rather than assume a coordinate convention. Is this a coincidence, or a real, generalizable lesson?
output: Treat convergent, independently-derived fixes to the same class of bug as strong evidence the underlying method is real and generalizable, not a coincidence. Axis/coordinate-frame mismatches (e.g. Z-up source data used inside a Y-up engine, or two rigs' own 'forward' directions disagreeing) are a recurring, structurally-similar failure mode across unrelated 3D pipelines. The real, transferable fix pattern: never assume a coordinate convention carries over unchanged between two systems - compute the actual transform from real data (landmark positions, mesh geometry, or a directly-measured reference axis), and verify the fix by hand-computing the expected error magnitude before trusting that a fix worked, not just confirming the symptom went away.

instruction: A game engine has one fixed, canonical character skeleton. Every imported 3D asset (a different game's character model, a scanned mesh, whatever) needs its geometry mapped onto that one skeleton before it can be posed/animated. Should the engine build a general-purpose bone-hierarchy editing tool so a human can re-parent/adjust bones on each new import by hand?
output: No - that's solving the wrong problem. If the target skeleton is fixed and canonical, the real per-import work is never 'edit a skeleton,' it's 'compute the mapping from this new source onto the one skeleton that already exists' - bone-name matching, which parts get their own source rotation trusted vs. reset, and a scale factor. Building a general hand-editing tool treats every import as a one-off manual task; the more scalable real design is a data-driven correction record (a real, reusable mapping: source bone name to target bone name, which bones' rotations are trustworthy, a mesh scale) that a human OR a sufficiently capable automated system can author once per source rig, resolved against each actual asset's real node names at load time so a mismatch is reported, not silently wrong. Once that authoring step itself can be automated (a system that understands spatial/structural reasoning about a skeleton well enough to propose the mapping itself), the tool needed is 'trust and verify a proposed mapping,' not 'manually re-parent bones' - a fundamentally smaller, more scalable capability than a general rig editor.

instruction: A compute call re-uploads the same large piece of data (e.g. a frozen weight matrix) to a separate device on every single invocation, even though that specific data never changes between calls - only a smaller, genuinely-different piece of the input does. Real per-call cost is dominated by the transfer, not the compute. What's the real, generalizable fix?
output: Cache the unchanging operand resident on the device, uploaded exactly once, and only transfer the genuinely-changing operand on every subsequent call. This is a real, broadly-applicable pattern, not specific to any one hardware API: identify which inputs are stable across repeated calls versus which are different every time, and only pay transfer cost for the latter. A real, measured example: caching a reused weight matrix on a GPU instead of re-uploading it every call cut real wall-clock by ~79% over 20 repeated calls, with the correctness proof being that both paths must produce byte-identical output - caching must never be allowed to silently change what's computed, only how expensively the same result is reached.

instruction: When adding a resource cache keyed by 'is this the same logical object as last time,' what's a real, robust way to derive the cache key, and what real property should gate whether an object is even eligible for caching in the first place?
output: A stable identity already present in the data - e.g. a reference-counted handle's own pointer address - is a real, robust cache key: the same real logical object (reused via cheap clone/reference, not deep-copied) always yields the same key, and a genuinely different object yields a different one, with no extra bookkeeping required from callers. Separately, real eligibility for caching should be gated on a property that actually signals stability, not just convenience - in a training system, a real, natural signal already exists: whether an object is marked as not needing gradient updates (frozen) versus needing them (actively changing). Caching an object that's marked as changing, even if its identity handle looks the same, would silently serve stale data - the gate must check the real stability property, not just object identity alone.

instruction: A real prior finding concluded that a specific limited hardware resource (2GB of VRAM on an old GPU) would provide only marginal benefit for a real workload, and that finding was correct and well-reasoned at the time. Later, real testing shows that same exact resource providing a large, measured benefit for what sounds like a similar workload. Is this a contradiction - was the earlier finding wrong?
output: Not necessarily a contradiction - check whether the two cases are using the resource under the same real architecture before assuming either finding is wrong. A real, concrete example: an earlier finding that 2GB VRAM gives only marginal benefit was specifically about a whole-layer-resident offload model, which genuinely cannot fit more than a small fraction of a real model's layers in that space at once - a real, correct conclusion for that specific memory model. A later finding that the same 2GB card gives a large, real, measured win used a structurally different approach: streaming one small operand at a time, never needing more than a few dozen megabytes resident at once, which sidesteps the exact capacity constraint the first finding was about. Two real, different architectures using the same physical resource can correctly reach different conclusions - the fix is to reconcile and document why both are true for their own case, not to assume the newer result overturned the older one, or ship the newer one without checking why the discrepancy exists.

instruction: Before assuming a piece of hardware (e.g. a specific GPU in a machine with more than one) is busy, contended, or unavailable for a purpose, what's the real, cheap first step to take?
output: Directly query the real, current state of that specific hardware rather than assume its role from general expectation. A real, concrete example: on a laptop with both an integrated and a discrete GPU, it's easy to assume the discrete (more powerful) card is the one handling display output, since that's the common general pattern - but the real, current state on one specific real machine was the opposite: the integrated GPU was confirmed (via a direct real OS query showing which adapter had a real active resolution set) to be the one driving the display, leaving the discrete GPU genuinely idle and free to dedicate entirely to a separate compute workload with zero real display contention. A cheap, direct check turned an assumption into a confirmed fact before it was relied on.

instruction: In a system with multiple layers or tiers of authority (e.g. a fast tactical tier and a slower strategic tier in a simulation, or any layered architecture), what's the real, generalizable rule for how data should flow between layers within a single processing step?
output: Orders flow down, state flows up - and no layer reads from a layer below it mid-step. A higher/slower tier may issue orders that a lower/faster tier executes, and the lower tier's resulting state becomes visible to the higher tier only at the boundary between steps, never read live mid-step. This is a real, generalizable unidirectional-flow discipline: it prevents a fast-changing lower layer from being observed in an inconsistent, half-updated state by a slower layer sharing the same step, and prevents circular dependencies between layers that would otherwise make step ordering ambiguous. The same shape applies well beyond simulation ticks - any system with a clear layering by update frequency or authority benefits from the same real discipline: command down, report up, no mid-step reach-around in either direction.

instruction: When both a numeric/measurable check and a subjective read (an AI's visual assessment, a human's visual impression) are available for the same real question, and they disagree, which should take priority?
output: The numeric, buildable, ground-truth check - a subjective visual read (from an AI or a human) is never treated as final when a real numeric check is available and disagrees with it. This is a real, standing precedence rule, distinct from the related but different lesson that numeric checks alone don't PROVE visual correctness (they can miss real visual defects a numeric check wouldn't catch) - this is about what to trust when the two SPECIFICALLY conflict: a real, measured number beats an impression, every time, because an impression can be wrong in ways that are hard to pin down, while a numeric check's own real methodology can be inspected and verified directly.

instruction: A capable but expensive shared resource (a premium AI model, a rate-limited API, a person's own limited attention) and a cheaper, more available one both exist. For a task that's mechanical and well-bounded (clear success criteria, no real judgment call needed), which should handle it, and why does this matter beyond just cost?
output: Route the mechanical, well-bounded task to the cheaper, more available resource, reserving the expensive/limited one for tasks that genuinely need its specific capability (real judgment calls, ambiguous cases, creative or high-stakes decisions). The real reason this matters beyond simple cost savings: an expensive or rate-limited resource used carelessly on tasks that didn't need it isn't just wasteful in isolation - it draws from the SAME finite budget that harder tasks will need later, so routine work quietly using it up is a real, compounding cost, not a one-off inefficiency. The discipline is to actually classify a task as mechanical-and-bounded versus judgment-requiring before assigning it, not default to the most capable resource out of convenience.

instruction: An immediate-mode GUI library hands back a real per-frame resource-delta object (e.g. texture updates that must be freed) each frame. A caller only reads/iterates that object's contents by reference and never calls its own explicit cleanup method. What happens, and what's the generalizable lesson?
output: A real crash - the object panics on drop, because iterating it by reference is not the same as telling it its contents were actually consumed. This came from a real bug getting a UI panel on screen for the first time: egui's own per-frame TexturesDelta type panics when dropped unless its own explicit .clear() (or equivalent real consumption method) is called, not just read. The generalizable rule: when a type's own API distinguishes between 'inspecting' and 'consuming/finalizing' a resource, reading it is never a substitute for the real finalization call - always check whether a returned per-frame/per-call resource object has its own required cleanup method, and call it explicitly, rather than assuming iteration alone was enough.

instruction: A one-shot, single-frame offscreen screenshot/capture of a live rendering system comes back wrong or empty on the very first real attempt, even though the same system looks completely correct when watched continuously in a live, running window. What's the generalizable explanation and fix?
output: A live, continuously-redrawing session hides real per-frame initialization work (e.g. a font atlas or shader warming up) because by the time a human actually looks at it, several real frames have already passed - but a single offscreen capture can land exactly on that real 'cold start' frame, with the initialization not yet complete (e.g. zero tessellated primitives). The real, generalizable fix is a deliberate throwaway warm-up pass - render one or more real frames and discard them before taking the actual capture - not a delay/sleep hack, which doesn't address the real cause (frames need to actually run, not just time need to pass) and is unreliable across different real hardware speeds. This is a real, structural gap between 'looks right interactively' and 'is right for a single automated capture' worth checking for in ANY continuously-redrawn system that also needs to support one-shot capture.

instruction: A simulated bipedal character (or a real bipedal robot) is losing balance. Real, established robotics control gives at least three named techniques of increasing sophistication for handling this - what are they, in order, and what does each one actually decide vs. actuate?
output: Three real, established techniques, from simplest to most complete: (1) Zero Moment Point (ZMP) - the ground point where the net moment of gravity plus inertial forces is zero; the real stability CONDITION is keeping the ZMP inside the support polygon (the convex hull of the feet in ground contact). ZMP is a real TARGET, not a force layer by itself - something else still has to move it back inside the polygon when it drifts out. (2) Whole-Body Control (WBC) - a real quadratic-program solve for joint torques/accelerations that satisfies several task objectives simultaneously (hold center-of-mass position, keep ZMP inside the polygon, track a desired pose) under real constraints (torque limits, unilateral ground-contact forces). This is real state-of-the-art for full humanoid robots but heavy machinery - a QP solve every tick, not a simple feedback loop. (3) Capture Point / Divergent Component of Motion - the real ground point that, if stepped on, brings the character (modeled as a Linear Inverted Pendulum) to a stop: c = x_com + (ẋ_com / ω), where ω = √(g/h). This answers a genuinely different, concrete question the other two don't: WHEN and WHERE to take a real recovery step, not just how to regulate standing balance. A real, practical layering: torque-based correction (a simpler PD approach) absorbs small disturbances; capture-point-driven stepping handles large ones the torque layer alone can't recover from - the two are complementary, not competing.

instruction: A real PD (proportional-derivative) motor is driving a joint in a physics simulation, and the real stiffness (kp) and damping (kd) gains need to be picked. Is there a real, practical rule of thumb for the ratio between them, and what happens at the extremes?
output: A real, practical rule of thumb: kd is approximately 0.1 times kp (kd ≈ 0.1 × kp), with kp itself typically in the real range of about 50 to 500 - larger, heavier joints (legs, spine) take the higher end of that range, smaller joints (arms, head) take the lower end. At the extremes: too-large kp causes real instability (the joint overshoots and oscillates); too-small kp causes real tracking error and starts behaving like a pure open-loop torque controller instead of a real position-tracking one. Too-small kd causes real instability from insufficient damping; too-large kd prevents the joint from actually tracking a moving target, since it resists velocity too strongly. A real, deliberate divergence from this ratio (e.g. a joint modeling a fast mechanical snap between two positions, wanting very high stiffness and very low damping) should be treated as an intentional, documented choice, not left unexplained - an unreconciled divergence from a known real rule of thumb is a real, standing open question until it's either justified or fixed.

instruction: A physics engine offers both a maximal-coordinate (impulse/constraint-based) joint solver and a reduced-coordinate (generalized/articulated) joint solver. Reduced-coordinate solvers are documented as guaranteeing zero real joint error 'by construction,' which sounds strictly better - but a real attempt to switch to one produced a severe real numerical explosion (NaN) that the maximal-coordinate solver never had, under the SAME real PD gains. Why, and what's required before retrying?
output: Reduced-coordinate articulated solvers explicitly integrate real Coriolis and centrifugal forces as part of their own formulation, but do NOT apply any automatic joint/body damping by default - a real, documented tradeoff for their zero-joint-error guarantee. A maximal-coordinate (impulse-based) solver's own real approximate, iterative constraint satisfaction incidentally provides a real damping-like stabilizing effect that a reduced-coordinate solver's mathematically exact formulation does not. This means empirically-tuned PD gains that were stable on the maximal-coordinate solver are NOT safe to reuse as-is on a reduced-coordinate solver - the real, required precondition before retrying is adding real velocity clamps and/or explicit extra damping first, not just lightly retuning the existing kp/kd values. The real, generalizable lesson: a solver's own real mathematical guarantees (here, zero joint error) can come with a real, different stability profile that isn't obvious from the guarantee alone, and gains tuned for one real solver architecture do not automatically transfer to a structurally different one.

instruction: A piece of hardware (e.g. a second GPU) crashes the whole process (a hard access violation, not a catchable error) when a specific code path is used. Two real, distinct bugs in that code path get found and fixed, and after both fixes, it works once. Then it fails again on the next several attempts with the identical crash. Should the earlier success be trusted as proof the hardware now works?
output: No - a single success surrounded by consistent failures (before AND after) is real evidence the success was a fluke (a transient race condition or driver state, not a repeatable capability), not proof of genuine working capability. The real, honest test is REPEATABILITY: re-run the identical code multiple times in a row. If it fails consistently again, the one success doesn't count as 'it works' - it counts as 'it can sometimes briefly appear to work, which is not the same as being reliable,' and unreliable hardware/driver behavior is often WORSE than it simply not working at all, especially for anything meant to run unattended for a long time, since an unpredictable hard crash can happen mid-task with no warning. A real, legitimate reset attempt (e.g. disabling and re-enabling the specific device, not just retrying the same code) is worth trying once as a real, direct test of whether the instability is session-state corruption versus a deeper, real hardware/driver limitation - if the crash is IDENTICAL before and after a real reset, that is real, strong evidence it's the latter, and the honest conclusion is to stop investigating and use a different, reliable resource instead, not to keep guessing at more code-level fixes for something that already survived two real, targeted fixes and a real reset without becoming reliable.

instruction: A real resource cache (e.g. one that keeps expensive-to-create objects resident so they don't need to be recreated every call) is built and verified: benchmarks confirm real, correct behavior AND a real, large speedup when the SAME single object is reused across many repeated calls. It's then wired into the real, full production system and immediately crashes with a real 'out of memory' error the very first time it runs. What real gap in the original verification caused this, and what's the generalizable lesson?
output: The original benchmarks only ever tested reusing ONE object many times - they never tested the AGGREGATE cost of caching MANY DISTINCT objects at once, which is exactly what the real, full production system does (e.g. 22 real, different layers' worth of weights, not one weight reused 22 times). An unbounded cache (no eviction, no size limit) that looks perfectly correct and fast when exercising a single cache entry can still blow through a real, hard memory ceiling once enough DISTINCT entries accumulate - the isolated benchmark's own real success said nothing about that failure mode, because it structurally couldn't produce it. The generalizable lesson: when verifying a cache or pool, test not just 'does reusing the same item work and stay correct,' but 'does the cache stay bounded when many genuinely different items are cached over the lifetime of a real, full run' - and the real, honest fix for an unbounded cache is a real, explicit memory budget (a hard byte cap, checked before every new insertion) with a defined, correct fallback (skip caching that one item, don't error) for when the budget would be exceeded, not an assumption that 'it worked in testing' generalizes to full-scale real use.

instruction: Across one real engineering session, three genuinely separate failures each led directly to a real, better outcome than if the original approach had simply worked on the first try: a crashing third-party tool forced building a component natively instead of depending on it; an unreliable second GPU forced developing and validating a real 'is this a fluke or a genuine capability' testing methodology; and an out-of-memory crash forced adding a real, explicit memory budget to a cache that would otherwise have been a silent, unbounded liability. Is this a coincidence, or a real, generalizable pattern worth acting on directly?
output: A real, generalizable pattern, not a coincidence - and the real, actionable consequence is: don't treat a failure as pure cost to be minimized and moved past as fast as possible. Investigate it properly BEFORE working around it, because the investigation itself regularly surfaces a real improvement that was never being looked for - a more owned, more robust, or more correct design than the one that would have shipped if the original attempt had simply succeeded. A crash that forces a system to be rebuilt natively ends up more maintainable than a dependency that happened to work. A driver that's flaky enough to force real reliability testing produces a reusable testing discipline. A cache that overflows and gets a real memory budget added is safer than a cache that never got tested against real-scale aggregate use and might have failed unpredictably in production much later, harder to diagnose. The real, standing implication for how to work: treat a setback as a real, direct signal to look closer, not a problem to route around quickly - the fix that comes out of understanding WHY something failed is usually better than a fix that just makes the symptom go away.

instruction: A real GPU crash produces only an opaque error type with no message of its own. Before assuming a cause and trying a fix, what real, concrete diagnostic steps should come first, and why does skipping them waste real effort?
output: First, use the platform's own real, specific diagnostic hooks instead of guessing from the opaque error alone - this project's wgpu case had THREE separate real mechanisms that each rule out a different class of cause: push_error_scope (Validation/OutOfMemory/Internal - each returning None ruled out every catchable API-level error), a device-lost callback (revealed the real underlying event was DeviceLost, a driver-level event none of the error scopes ever catch), and real wall-clock timing around the failing call (37.5ms, definitively ruling out a slow-dispatch/timeout theory that looked plausible on paper but had zero real timing evidence behind it). Each of these took only a few lines of code and immediately eliminated an entire category of hypothesis with real data, rather than a guess. The generalizable lesson: an opaque error is a prompt to ask 'what real, specific diagnostic capability does this exact system expose for this exact failure class' before spending time on a plausible-sounding but unverified theory - a wrong hypothesis pursued for an hour costs far more than five minutes spent finding the right diagnostic hook first.

instruction: A real, hard-to-reproduce bug only manifests inside a large, complex, real system - never in any isolated benchmark or unit test built to reproduce it, even after several honest, well-targeted attempts. What's the real, correct way to keep making progress, and what's the wrong instinct to resist?
output: The wrong instinct is to keep constructing new isolated repros indefinitely on pure guesswork, each one a slightly different combination of assumed variables, hoping one eventually lands - this can burn real, unbounded time with no guarantee of ever converging, since a growing repro that tries to replicate 'the whole real system' stops being an isolation at all. The real, correct move once several honest, targeted repro attempts have failed: go back to the REAL, actual failure - not a truncated summary of it, the full, untruncated evidence - and read ALL of it carefully, including parts that seemed unimportant on a first pass. In this project's own case, a real allocation-event log had already been captured from the real crash, but only a truncated notification of it had been read; the specific pattern that actually explained the bug (two ~250MB buffer creates immediately preceding every failure) was sitting, unread, in the last ~15% of that log the whole time. The generalizable lesson: when synthetic reproduction attempts keep failing, the fastest real path forward is usually re-examining the complete real evidence you already have more carefully, not generating more speculative isolated scenarios - the answer is very often already captured, just not yet fully read.
